questions.stem: How do water molecules orient around a sodium ion during solvation?

options.text: Their partially negative oxygen regions face the positive sodium ion
options.why: A positive ion attracts the partially negative region of polar water. The surrounding water molecules help keep the ion dispersed.

options.text: Their partially positive hydrogen regions face the positive sodium ion
options.why: The hydrogen regions also carry partial positive charges, so this orientation doesn't produce the relevant attraction. They face negative ions.

options.text: Their oxygen atoms form covalent bonds directly with the sodium ion
options.why: Solvation doesn't require new covalent bonds. It uses electrostatic attraction between the ion and water's partial charges.

options.text: Their hydrogen atoms remove an electron and convert sodium into a neutral atom
options.why: Sodium remains an ion in the solution. Water surrounds and disperses it without neutralizing its charge.

questions.stem: A membrane separates a 0.2 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution from a 0.7 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution and permits water, but not sucrose, to cross. What is the net movement?

options.text: Water moves from the 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution to the 0.7 mol dm⁻³ solution
options.why: The 0.2 mol dm⁻³ side is hypotonic and the 0.7 mol dm⁻³ side is hypertonic. Net water movement is toward the higher solute concentration.

options.text: Water moves from the 0.7 mol dm⁻³ solution to the 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution
options.why: That direction runs from the hypertonic solution toward the hypotonic one. Osmosis produces net water movement in the opposite direction here.

options.text: Sucrose moves from the 0.7 mol dm⁻³ solution to the 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution
options.why: That would describe diffusion of sucrose, but the membrane in the question prevents sucrose from crossing. Water is the substance moving.

options.text: Water and sucrose move together until both sides contain 0.45 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
options.why: Sucrose can't cross this membrane, so both substances don't move together. Only water can redistribute between the sides.

questions.stem: What happens to water at isotonic equilibrium across a cell membrane?

options.text: Water crosses in both directions at equal rates
options.why: This is dynamic equilibrium. Individual molecules keep moving, but equal rates give no net movement.

options.text: All movement of water across the membrane stops
options.why: Molecular motion continues at equilibrium. The rates in opposite directions become equal rather than falling to zero.

options.text: Water enters while solute leaves at the same rate
options.why: Isotonic equilibrium concerns equal water movement in opposite directions. It doesn't require an exchange of water for solute.

options.text: Water leaves until the cell has no dissolved solutes
options.why: An isotonic environment causes no net loss of water. The cell's solutes remain present.

questions.stem: A red blood cell is placed in a strongly hypertonic solution. What happens?

options.text: It loses water and becomes crenated
options.why: The surrounding solution has the higher solute concentration, so net water movement is out. The animal cell shrinks and becomes crenated.

options.text: It gains water and bursts by lysis
options.why: Lysis is expected in a sufficiently hypotonic solution, where net water movement is into a cell lacking a wall.

options.text: It develops turgor pressure against its wall
options.why: Red blood cells lack cell walls. Turgor pressure develops in walled cells as their contents press outward.

options.text: It becomes plasmolyzed as its membrane leaves the wall
options.why: Plasmolysis requires a cell wall from which the membrane can separate. A red blood cell becomes crenated instead.

questions.stem: Why does a plant cell usually become turgid rather than burst in a hypotonic solution?

options.text: Its wall resists expansion as rising pressure opposes further water entry
options.why: Water entry pushes the contents against the wall, producing turgor pressure. Rising pressure potential brings the cell toward water-potential equilibrium.

options.text: Its wall prevents any water from crossing the cell membrane
options.why: Water still crosses the membrane. The wall limits expansion after water has entered; it isn't an impermeable barrier around the cell.

options.text: Its chloroplasts use the incoming water during photosynthesis immediately
options.why: Photosynthesis doesn't remove incoming water rapidly enough to explain the stable volume. Mechanical resistance from the wall produces the pressure.

options.text: Its vacuole pumps every excess water molecule back into the solution
options.why: A plant vacuole helps store water but doesn't expel it like a contractile vacuole. Turgor pressure limits further net entry.

questions.stem: Which observation identifies the isotonic concentration in a plant-tissue investigation?

options.text: Zero mean percentage change in tissue mass
options.why: Zero change indicates no net water gain or loss. On a graph, this is the concentration at the x-intercept.

options.text: The greatest final mass among the tissue samples
options.why: The greatest final mass usually indicates substantial water uptake. Isotonic conditions produce no change from the initial mass.

options.text: The lowest standard deviation among all concentrations
options.why: A low standard deviation shows tightly grouped repeats. It doesn't identify where net water movement was zero.

options.text: Equal initial masses for every tissue sample
options.why: Equal starting masses improve control but don't reveal the isotonic concentration. The change after treatment provides that evidence.

questions.stem: Why do many freshwater unicellular organisms need contractile vacuoles?

options.text: Water enters continually by osmosis and must be expelled
options.why: Fresh water is hypotonic relative to the cell contents. The vacuole removes incoming water and reduces the risk of excessive swelling.

options.text: Solutes enter continually by diffusion and must be digested
options.why: A contractile vacuole regulates excess water rather than digesting solutes. Digestion occurs in other compartments.

options.text: Water leaves continually, so the vacuole replaces the loss
options.why: In fresh water, the net direction is into the organism. The vacuole expels water rather than supplying it.

options.text: The cell wall needs pressure generated by repeated contractions
options.why: Many organisms using contractile vacuoles don't rely on a plant-like wall. The contractions remove excess water from the cell.

questions.stem: Why should an intravenous fluid be isotonic with blood plasma?

options.text: It prevents net osmosis that could shrink or lyse blood cells
options.why: An isotonic fluid maintains cell volume because water moves both ways at equal rates. This avoids harmful swelling or shrinking.

options.text: It stops every water molecule from crossing blood-cell membranes
options.why: Water continues crossing in both directions. Isotonic conditions prevent net movement, not molecular movement.

options.text: It causes red blood cells to develop protective turgor pressure
options.why: Red blood cells have no wall and don't become turgid. Isotonic fluid keeps their volume near its normal value.

options.text: It draws excess water from cells so their metabolism accelerates
options.why: Drawing water out would require a hypertonic fluid and would make cells shrink. That isn't the purpose of an intravenous solution.

options.text: The potential energy of water per unit volume
options.why: Water potential describes the potential energy of water relative to a reference state and is usually measured in kilopascals.

options.text: The number of water molecules in each unit volume
options.why: That's a description of concentration. Water potential is an energy quantity per unit volume.

options.text: The pressure needed to stop every water molecule moving
options.why: Water molecules never have to stop moving. Water potential predicts the direction of net movement.

options.text: The kinetic energy released when water crosses a membrane
options.why: Water potential concerns potential energy, not kinetic energy released during membrane crossing.

questions.stem: A cell has Ψs = −1,100 kPa and Ψp = +700 kPa. What is its water potential?

options.text: −400 kPa
options.why: Using Ψw = Ψs + Ψp gives −1,100 kPa + 700 kPa = −400 kPa.
This results from subtracting the positive pressure potential. The equation requires the two signed values to be added.

options.text: +400 kPa
options.why: The magnitude is obtained from the two values, but the negative solute contribution remains larger than the positive pressure contribution.
Adding the magnitudes and making the result positive ignores both signs in the water-potential equation.

questions.stem: Two compartments have water potentials of −300 kPa and −850 kPa. What is the direction of net water movement?

options.text: From −300 kPa to −850 kPa
options.why: The value −300 kPa is higher because it's less negative. Water moves from higher to lower water potential.

options.text: From −850 kPa to −300 kPa
options.why: This runs from lower to higher water potential. A larger negative magnitude doesn't mean a higher potential.

options.text: In neither direction because both values are negative
options.why: Negative values can still form a gradient. Their unequal values predict net movement toward −850 kPa.

options.text: Equally in both directions because the difference is pressure
options.why: The values given are unequal total water potentials. Equal opposing rates occur only at water-potential equilibrium.

questions.stem: Why can pressure potential in a xylem vessel be negative?

options.text: Transpiration places the column of xylem sap under tension
options.why: Evaporation from leaves pulls on the continuous water column. Tension makes the pressure contribution negative.

options.text: Dissolved mineral ions always make physical pressure negative
options.why: Dissolved particles make solute potential negative. They don't automatically give the sap a negative pressure potential.

options.text: Xylem walls actively pump water upward using metabolic energy
options.why: Xylem vessels are dead at maturity and don't pump water. Transpiration generates the tension.

options.text: Gravity removes all potential energy from water inside the vessel
options.why: Negative pressure here comes from tension in the sap. It doesn't mean that the water has lost all potential energy.
